claims.text: Steels with sufficient chromium content form a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 passive film during controlled thermal oxidation.
A continuous Cr2O3 passive film impedes the ingress of corrosive ions.
The Cr2O3 film enhances corrosion resistance relative to low-chromium steels.
Thermal oxidation at 400–600 °C in air or oxygen can induce formation of a protective Cr2O3 film on the proposed steels.
The relevant structural mediator is a uniform, chromium-rich Cr2O3 passivating layer on the steel surface.
High chromium content enables development of a stable, protective Cr2O3 layer during controlled thermal oxidation.
The Cr2O3 layer acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
Chromium-deficient steels fail to form protective oxide films under the proposed treatment.
Failure to form a protective film results in higher corrosion rates.
Steels with optimal chromium levels and properly formed Cr2O3 films will have lower overall corrosion rates than low-chromium steels.
Steels with optimal chromium levels and properly formed Cr2O3 films will have lower localized corrosion rates than low-chromium steels.
The proposed low-chromium controls will not develop a continuous Cr2O3 film under the same oxidation treatment.
The mechanism is expected to apply across chromium ranges typical of both low-alloy and 300-series stainless steels.
The mechanism is expected to apply under thermal oxidation conditions of 400–600 °C.
An absence of correlation among chromium content, film quality, and corrosion performance would falsify the hypothesis.
Formation by low-chromium samples of films similar in quality to those on high-chromium samples would falsify the proposed chromium-dependent mechanism.
No discernible corrosion-resistance difference despite variation in chromium content would falsify the hypothesis.
